skill: Explaining the purpose of the Enterprise Project Structure (EPS) in P6
question: In Primavera P6, what is the primary purpose of the Enterprise Project Structure (EPS)?

options.label: A
options.text: To organize all projects in the database into a hierarchy for portfolio-level grouping, security, and reporting

options.label: B
options.text: To break a single project's scope of work into deliverables and packages

options.label: C
options.text: To list every activity code value available to a project

options.label: D
options.text: To define the calendars available for scheduling activities

explanation: The EPS is the top-level hierarchy that organizes every project in the P6 database (by division, region, business line, etc.). Projects reside inside EPS nodes; the EPS itself never holds activities. Breaking down a single project's scope is the job of the project's own Work Breakdown Structure (WBS), not the EPS.
reasoning: P6 separates portfolio-level organization (EPS, used for grouping many projects and controlling access via OBS-linked security) from project-level scope decomposition (WBS, unique to each project). Confusing the two is one of the most common fundamentals mistakes new users make.
commonMistakes: Believing the EPS is where individual activities or WBS elements live.
Treating EPS nodes as if they were projects themselves.
p6Checks: EPS window (Enterprise > Enterprise Project Structure) shows the node hierarchy; projects are added underneath specific nodes.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How does the EPS relate to the OBS for security purposes?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate connects EPS placement to project access control via OBS-linked security profiles.

skill: Distinguishing an EPS node from a Project
question: True or False: In Primavera P6, activities can be added directly to an EPS node without first creating a project underneath it.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: False. Activities can only exist inside a project (and within that project's WBS). An EPS node is purely an organizational container for projects; it has no activities, calendars, or WBS of its own. You must create a project under an EPS node before any activity data can be entered.
reasoning: The EPS-Project-WBS-Activity hierarchy is strict: EPS holds Projects, Projects hold WBS elements, WBS elements hold Activities. Skipping a level is not possible in the data model.
commonMistakes: Assuming EPS nodes are interchangeable with projects because both appear in the same tree view.
p6Checks: Try adding an activity while an EPS node (not a project) is selected in the Activities view filter bar – no activities will be available to add.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is the full hierarchy from EPS down to an individual activity?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Remedial check on the core data model.

skill: Applying OBS to assign management responsibility and control access
scenario: On a 900-activity data center build, the client wants each WBS element (Civil, Structural, Electrical, Mechanical, Fit-Out) to show which manager is accountable for it, and wants those same managers restricted so they can only edit activities under their own WBS elements when they log into P6.
question: Which P6 structure should the planner use to achieve this, and how does it get applied to the WBS elements?
expectedAnswer: Use the Organizational Breakdown Structure (OBS). Create an OBS hierarchy matching the management structure (e.g., Civil Manager, Structural Manager, Electrical Manager, etc.), then assign the relevant OBS element as the 'Responsible Manager' on each WBS element (WBS Details > General tab, Responsible Manager field). Combine this with Project security profiles tied to each OBS element so each manager's login is restricted to editing only the WBS elements their OBS node is responsible for.
strongAnswer: Notes that OBS-to-WBS assignment alone only displays responsibility for reporting; actual edit restriction requires configuring a User's Project security profile scoped to that OBS element (Admin > Security Profiles / Users, assigning the OBS element under 'Project Access').
expertAnswer: Flags that OBS should mirror the real accountability structure (not the WBS breakdown) so that responsibility and access rights survive WBS reorganizations, and that over-restricting access can block legitimate cross-discipline coordination (e.g., an MEP manager needing to see, but not edit, Structural logic that MEP work depends on).
explanation: The OBS represents the management/organizational hierarchy, independent of the WBS (which represents the deliverable/scope breakdown). Each WBS element can be assigned a single Responsible Manager from the OBS. Security profiles are then linked to OBS elements to control who can view/edit which part of the project.
reasoning: P6 deliberately keeps OBS and WBS as separate structures so that reorganizing scope (WBS) does not require rebuilding the responsibility/security model (OBS), and so the same OBS can be reused across many projects.
commonMistakes: Confusing OBS with Activity Codes used for a 'Responsible Engineer' text label.
Assuming assigning a Responsible Manager on the WBS automatically restricts that manager's edit rights without also configuring security profiles.
redFlags: Cannot distinguish OBS (org/security) from WBS (scope) at all.
p6Checks: WBS view > WBS Details > General tab > Responsible Manager field.
Enterprise > OBS to build/verify the OBS hierarchy.
Admin > Security Profiles and User accounts to confirm OBS-linked project access restrictions.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What happens to the security restriction if a manager needs read-only visibility into another discipline's activities?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of view vs edit access nuances.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that OBS and WBS are intentionally independent hierarchies.

skill: Choosing OBS versus an Activity Code to represent responsibility depending on the reporting need
scenario: A planning lead is setting up a highway widening project. The client wants two different things: (1) formal management accountability per WBS package that also drives who can edit what in P6, and (2) the ability to filter/group individual activities by which discipline crew (Paving, Drainage, Signage, Landscaping) is executing them, where a single WBS package can contain activities from several different crews.
question: Should the planning lead use the OBS, an Activity Code, or both to satisfy these two requirements? Justify the choice for each requirement.
expectedAnswer: Use OBS for requirement (1): it assigns one Responsible Manager per WBS element and, combined with security profiles, controls edit access – exactly the accountability/security use case. Use an Activity Code (e.g., 'Discipline Crew') for requirement (2): Activity Codes are assigned per activity (not per WBS element), so activities from different crews sitting inside the same WBS package can each carry their own code value and be grouped/filtered/reported independently of WBS structure.
strongAnswer: Notes that OBS assignment is coarse (one value per WBS element, inherited conceptually by everything under it) while Activity Codes are granular (one value per activity), which is exactly why mixed-discipline WBS packages need codes, not OBS, for crew-level reporting.
expertAnswer: Adds that using both together is standard practice on multi-discipline projects: OBS drives who is accountable and what they can edit, while Activity Codes drive cross-cutting reporting views (e.g., 'show me all Drainage activities across every WBS package') that WBS/OBS structure alone cannot produce because WBS is a single fixed hierarchy.
explanation: OBS answers 'who is responsible/who can edit this part of the project' at the WBS-element level and ties into security. Activity Codes answer 'how do I classify and slice individual activities' for filtering, grouping, and reporting, independent of the WBS hierarchy. They solve different problems and are commonly used together, not as substitutes for each other.
reasoning: A WBS package is a single node that can only have one Responsible Manager; it cannot represent four different crews working inside it. Activity Codes exist precisely because reporting often needs to cut across the WBS/OBS hierarchy (e.g., 'all Paving work' regardless of which WBS package it sits in).
commonMistakes: Trying to force OBS to do activity-level classification by creating an OBS node per crew and reassigning WBS elements repeatedly.
Using Activity Codes for security/access control, which they cannot provide.
redFlags: Proposes restructuring the WBS itself around crews just to get crew-level reporting, when an Activity Code solves it without touching the WBS.
p6Checks: Enterprise > Activity Codes to create a project- or EPS-level 'Discipline Crew' code with one value per crew.
WBS Details > General tab > Responsible Manager to confirm OBS assignment per package.
Activities view > Group and Sort by the new Activity Code to verify cross-WBS grouping works.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of Activity Codes (shared, enterprise pick-list, good for grouping) vs UDFs (per-activity free values, weaker for standardized grouping).

skill: Distinguishing the project's WBS from the enterprise-wide EPS
question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a project's WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) and the EPS (Enterprise Project Structure) in P6?

options.label: A
options.text: The WBS is a hierarchy unique to each individual project, used to break its scope into deliverables/packages; the EPS is a separate, database-wide hierarchy used to organize multiple projects

options.label: B
options.text: The WBS and EPS are the same structure, just viewed from two different windows

options.label: C
options.text: The EPS is nested inside the WBS of the top-level project

options.label: D
options.text: A project can only have a WBS if it also has a matching EPS node created specifically for it

explanation: The WBS lives inside a single project and decomposes that project's scope of work into packages/deliverables, ultimately down to activities. The EPS sits above all projects in the database and is used purely to organize/group many projects for portfolio reporting and security – it is a completely separate hierarchy from any project's WBS.
reasoning: P6's data model deliberately separates 'how is this one project's scope broken down' (WBS) from 'how are all my projects organized as a portfolio' (EPS). Every project has exactly one WBS root (usually mirroring the project itself) but sits under whichever EPS node it was created in.
commonMistakes: Treating EPS and WBS as synonyms because both are tree/hierarchy views in the P6 interface.
p6Checks: WBS view (within a single open project) versus the separate EPS window (Enterprise > Enterprise Project Structure, spanning the whole database).

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can two different projects share the same WBS codes at their top level? Does that cause a conflict?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that WBS is scoped per project and does not need to be globally unique.

skill: Interpreting how a WBS Summary activity's dates are automatically calculated
scenario: On a marine terminal project, a planner adds an activity called 'Berth 2 – Overall Summary' with Activity Type set to WBS Summary, placed at the same WBS level as the detailed dredging, piling, and deck-pour activities for Berth 2. After running the schedule (F9), the planner tries to manually type a Start date directly into that WBS Summary activity's Start field, but P6 will not accept the manual entry.
question: Why can't the planner manually edit the WBS Summary activity's dates, and what actually determines its Start and Finish?
explanation: A WBS Summary activity's dates are not independently scheduled – they are automatically derived by P6 as the span from the earliest Start among the detail activities that share its WBS level (or the subset defined by its assigned filter/code) to the latest Finish among those same activities. Because the dates are a computed rollup rather than a scheduled result of relationships and durations, P6 does not allow direct manual date entry on a WBS Summary activity; the only way to change its dates is to change the dates of the underlying detail activities it summarizes.
reasoning: WBS Summary is one of P6's activity types specifically built for rollup/reporting bars rather than for CPM calculation – it has no duration logic of its own and does not participate in the forward/backward pass like Task Dependent or Resource Dependent activities do; it simply reflects whatever the current earliest-start/latest-finish envelope of its group is after each schedule run.
commonMistakes: Assuming WBS Summary activities can be constrained or manually dated like normal activities.
Believing a WBS Summary activity drives or is driven by relationships the same way Task Dependent activities are.
redFlags: Recommends adding a constraint to 'fix' the WBS Summary's date instead of recognizing it is a computed rollup.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – Activity Type field showing 'WBS Summary'.
Confirm which WBS level/activities the summary is rolling up by checking the WBS assignment of the detail activities.
Re-run F9 after changing a detail activity's dates and observe the WBS Summary bar move automatically.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate conflates the WBS Summary activity type with the WBS hierarchy node.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that WBS Summary activities are reporting rollups, not part of true CPM float calculations.

skill: Predicting auto-generated Activity IDs from the project's prefix/suffix/increment defaults
scenario: In Project Details > Defaults, the Activity ID auto-numbering is configured with Prefix 'ELEC', a starting Suffix of 1010, and an Increment of 10. The planner has already added activities ELEC1010, ELEC1020, and ELEC1030 using the auto-numbering default.
question: If the planner adds one more new activity using the auto-numbering default (without editing it manually), what Activity ID will P6 assign?
explanation: P6 auto-generates the next Activity ID by taking the last-used suffix number and adding the configured Increment. The last suffix used was 1030, so the next one is 1030 + 10 = 1040, giving ELEC1040.
reasoning: Auto-numbering simply tracks the highest suffix number assigned so far under that prefix and adds the increment each time a new activity is created, regardless of the order activities appear in the Activities view.
commonMistakes: Assuming the increment restarts from the original starting suffix (1010) instead of continuing from the last used number.
Forgetting to include the prefix in the answer.
p6Checks: Project Details > Defaults tab – Activity ID Prefix, Suffix, and Increment fields.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the planner manually renames one activity to ELEC9999, does that change what the auto-numbering suggests next?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that auto-numbering tracks the actual highest suffix in use, including manually entered IDs.

skill: Resolving duplicate Activity IDs after merging or importing schedules without breaking logic
scenario: Two subcontractor schedules for a hospital fit-out (Mechanical and Electrical) were each built independently with the same default Activity ID scheme, so both contain activities named A1000 through A1200. The lead planner imports both into a single integrated master project and now sees duplicate Activity ID warnings/conflicts.
question: What is the correct way to resolve the duplicate Activity IDs without damaging the relationships already built into either subcontractor schedule?
explanation: The planner should use P6's Renumber Activity IDs function on one (or both) of the imported activity sets – selecting the Mechanical activities (or Electrical activities) and applying a new prefix and/or starting number/increment. Renumbering changes only the Activity ID field; it does not touch the underlying relationships, which P6 tracks internally, so predecessor/successor logic, constraints, and resource assignments remain intact after the rename.
reasoning: Activity ID is just a display/reference label; P6's internal relationship data is not keyed off the visible ID text, so bulk renumbering a whole set of activities is safe and is the standard way to de-duplicate IDs after combining schedules from different sources.
commonMistakes: Manually retyping IDs one by one, risking typos that break intended grouping/filtering by ID pattern.
Deleting and re-creating activities to get new IDs, which would actually destroy the existing relationships and progress.
Assuming duplicate IDs are harmless and can be left as-is.
redFlags: Proposes deleting and rebuilding activities to fix an ID conflict.
p6Checks: Select the activities to renumber in the Activities view, then use Edit > Renumber Activity IDs (or right-click context menu) and specify a new prefix/suffix/increment.
After renumbering, spot-check a sample of relationships and resource assignments to confirm nothing else changed.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that Activity IDs only need to be unique within one project, so the conflict here only matters because both sets now live in the same integrated project.

skill: Recognizing that Task Dependent activities are governed by their own activity calendar, not by assigned resource calendars
scenario: On a retail fit-out project, activity 'Install Shopfront Glazing' is set to Activity Type = Task Dependent and assigned to the project's Standard 5-Day calendar. A specialist glazing subcontractor resource, who personally works a 4-day week (their individual resource calendar excludes Fridays), is assigned to the activity.
question: Will this activity's schedule dates be affected by the glazing subcontractor's 4-day resource calendar?

options.label: A
options.text: No – as a Task Dependent activity, its dates are driven entirely by the activity's own assigned calendar (Standard 5-Day), regardless of the resource's personal calendar

options.label: B
options.text: Yes – Task Dependent activities always default to the calendar of whichever resource has the fewest working days

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only if the resource is the primary resource on the activity

options.label: D
options.text: It depends on the Duration Type selected for the activity

explanation: Task Dependent is P6's default activity type where the activity's own assigned calendar governs its scheduled dates, independent of the calendars of any resources assigned to it. Only Resource Dependent activities let individual resource calendars drive the activity's dates.
reasoning: The activity type setting is precisely what tells P6 which calendar to use for the forward/backward pass: Task Dependent uses the Activity Calendar field; Resource Dependent uses each assigned resource's own calendar instead.
commonMistakes: Assuming any resource's personal calendar automatically overrides the activity calendar regardless of activity type.
Confusing this with Duration Type, which governs the effort/units/duration relationship, not which calendar drives dates.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – confirm Activity Type = Task Dependent and check the assigned Calendar field.
Compare against how the same activity would behave if switched to Resource Dependent.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If this activity were switched to Resource Dependent, how would the schedule calculation change?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can articulate the actual mechanical difference between the two activity types.

skill: Diagnosing an activity's finish date driven by an individual resource's calendar rather than the assigned activity calendar
scenario: On an offshore wind cable-pull project, activity 'Pull and Terminate Export Cable' is Activity Type = Resource Dependent, with Activity Calendar shown as 'Standard 6-Day Workweek'. Two resources are assigned: a Cable Jointer (personal resource calendar = 5-day week, no weekend work) and a Survey Technician (personal resource calendar = 6-day week). After scheduling, the activity's finish date lands two days later than the planner expected based on the 6-Day activity calendar shown on the General tab.
question: What is the most likely explanation for the later-than-expected finish date, and what should the planner check?
explanation: Because the activity is Resource Dependent, P6 does not use the Activity Calendar field shown on the General tab to drive dates – it uses each assigned resource's own individual calendar for that resource's portion of the work, and the overall activity dates are governed by the resource that needs the longest calendar time to complete its assigned Units. Here, the Cable Jointer's 5-day calendar has less available working time per week than the 6-day calendar the planner was mentally using, so the Jointer's work (and therefore the activity) takes longer in calendar terms, pushing the finish out by roughly the extra non-working day(s) accumulated over the duration.
reasoning: Resource Dependent activity type exists specifically so that each assigned resource can work to its own calendar independently; the displayed Activity Calendar field becomes informational only (or governs any unresourced portion) once the type is Resource Dependent, and P6 schedules the overall activity to encompass the longest-running resource assignment.
commonMistakes: Reading the Activity Calendar field on the General tab and assuming it drives the schedule regardless of activity type.
Assuming all resources on a Resource Dependent activity finish together automatically.
redFlags: Insists on changing the Activity Calendar field to '5-Day' to 'fix' the date without checking individual resource calendars first, potentially masking the real driver.
p6Checks: Activity Details > Resources tab – review each assigned resource and check its individual calendar via the resource dictionary (Enterprise > Resources > General tab > Calendar).
Confirm Activity Type is genuinely Resource Dependent on the General tab.
Compare each resource assignment's own Start/Finish (visible on the Resources tab or Resource Usage Spreadsheet) to see which resource is driving the later finish.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the planner needs the activity to finish on the 6-day calendar dates, what are the options?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate proposes realistic fixes – e.g., aligning the Cable Jointer's resource calendar, changing activity type, or splitting the scope – rather than a cosmetic fix.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Would switching this activity to Task Dependent change how it schedules, and is that the right fix here?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands the trade-off of losing per-resource calendar driving if they switch activity type.

skill: Understanding that a Level of Effort activity's dates are entirely derived from its driving relationships
scenario: A planner creates activity 'Site Supervision & QA/QC Support' with Activity Type = Level of Effort (LOE), tied with a Start-to-Start relationship to the first foundation activity and a Finish-to-Finish relationship to the final handover activity. The planner then tries to manually shorten the LOE activity's Original Duration to '30d' to cap the supervision budget, expecting the activity to now finish 30 working days after it starts regardless of the handover date.
question: Is it possible for a Level of Effort activity's duration to behave that way – fixed at a manually entered value independent of its relationships?
explanation: No. An LOE activity's Duration is not an independent input the way it is for Task Dependent or Resource Dependent activities – it is automatically recalculated on every schedule run to span exactly from its earliest driving predecessor date to its latest driving successor date. Manually typing '30d' into the Duration field will not hold; the next time F9 is run, P6 recalculates the LOE's duration to match whatever span its Start-to-Start and Finish-to-Finish relationships currently produce, so it will stretch or shrink automatically as the foundation start date or handover finish date move.
reasoning: LOE activities exist specifically to represent effort that continues for the duration of other work (supervision, QA/QC, project management support) rather than effort with its own fixed scope of work; P6 implements this by making LOE duration a dependent, calculated output of its relationships rather than an independent scheduled value.
commonMistakes: Assuming Duration behaves the same way for every activity type.
Trying to use Duration or a constraint to cap an LOE activity's length instead of managing the relationships or budget driving it.
redFlags: Recommends adding a Finish constraint to 'lock' the LOE duration without recognizing this conflicts with the activity type's intended behavior.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – confirm Activity Type = Level of Effort.
Activity Details > Relationships tab – identify the driving predecessor/successor relationships that define the LOE's span.
Run F9 after manually editing Duration and observe that it recalculates back to the relationship-driven span.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate proposes a realistic alternative (e.g., managing it through resource budget/units or splitting scope) instead of fighting the activity type's core behavior.

skill: Diagnosing an LOE activity with frozen or unrealistic dates due to a missing or incorrect driving relationship
scenario: On a pharmaceutical plant qualification project, 'Project Management Support' is an LOE activity that should span the entire execution phase. After the latest schedule update, it still shows the very first Data Date from six months ago as its Finish date, even though the project is clearly still active and dozens of downstream activities have since progressed well past that date.
question: What is the most likely cause of the LOE activity's Finish date being stuck so far in the past, and how would you confirm it?
explanation: The most likely cause is that the LOE activity has lost (or never had) a valid driving successor relationship – for example, its Finish-to-Finish link to the project's closeout/handover activity was deleted, broken during a logic revision, or was never created, or the linked successor itself is an out-of-sequence/inactive activity that isn't producing a meaningful late date. Without a live driving successor, P6 has nothing current to span to, so the LOE's calculated Finish can be left anchored to whatever it last successfully derived from – which can look 'frozen' near an old date.
reasoning: LOE dates are entirely a function of the driving predecessor/successor relationships present at schedule time; if those relationships are missing, broken, or pointing at something that itself isn't updating, the LOE has no valid input to compute a current span from.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is a data date problem alone rather than checking the relationship logic first.
Manually re-dating the LOE activity to 'fix' the symptom instead of restoring the driving relationship.
redFlags: Manually types a new Finish date onto the LOE activity without investigating why the relationship-driven calculation isn't producing a current date, effectively masking a logic defect.
p6Checks: Activity Details > Relationships tab on the LOE activity – verify a live Start-to-Start and Finish-to-Finish (or equivalent) relationship still exists to activities that are themselves being actively updated.
Check whether the linked successor activity is itself Inactive, out-of-sequence, or has a constraint suppressing its own date movement.
Run F9 and watch whether the LOE recalculates once the relationship is corrected.

skill: Distinguishing Start Milestone from Finish Milestone activity types
question: What is the key functional difference between a Start Milestone and a Finish Milestone activity type in P6?

options.label: A
options.text: A Start Milestone only has a Start date and no Finish date; a Finish Milestone only has a Finish date and no Start date – both have zero duration

options.label: B
options.text: A Start Milestone can have resources assigned but a Finish Milestone cannot

options.label: C
options.text: A Start Milestone marks the beginning of the project; a Finish Milestone can only be used once per project, at the very end

options.label: D
options.text: There is no functional difference – it is purely a labeling/reporting choice

explanation: Both Start Milestone and Finish Milestone are zero-duration activity types, but they differ in which single date they represent and display: a Start Milestone activity has only a Start date (its 'finish' is the same instant), while a Finish Milestone activity has only a Finish date. Neither is limited to a single use per project or exclusively tied to the project start/end – both can be used freely anywhere in the schedule to mark a point-in-time event (e.g., 'Design Freeze' as a Finish Milestone, 'Site Mobilization Begins' as a Start Milestone).
reasoning: Milestones exist to flag a discrete point in time rather than a span of work; the Start/Finish distinction simply determines which side of that instant P6 treats as the governing date for relationship logic (e.g., a predecessor relationship into a Finish Milestone typically ties to its Finish, not a separate Start).
commonMistakes: Assuming milestones are restricted to project start/end.
Believing there's a meaningful difference in resource assignment rules between the two milestone types.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – Activity Type dropdown showing Start Milestone / Finish Milestone options.

followUpQuestions.prompt: Can a milestone have a non-zero duration entered by mistake, and what happens if someone tries?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate knows P6 forces milestone duration to zero regardless of manual entry attempts.

skill: Recognizing that WBS Summary activity dates are read-only, auto-computed values
question: True or False: The Start and Finish dates shown for a WBS Summary activity are automatically calculated by P6 and cannot be directly typed in by the user.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: True. A WBS Summary activity's dates are a computed rollup (earliest Start to latest Finish) of the detail activities under its WBS level, refreshed on every schedule run. It is not a normally scheduled activity, so it does not accept manually typed dates or constraints the way Task Dependent, Resource Dependent, or milestone activities do.
reasoning: WBS Summary exists purely as a reporting rollup activity type; giving it independently editable dates would let it disagree with the very activities it's supposed to summarize.
commonMistakes: Assuming any activity's date fields are always directly editable regardless of activity type.

skill: Choosing between an Activity Code and a User Defined Field for a given data-capture requirement
scenario: A planner on an airport terminal expansion needs to capture two things on every activity: (1) which construction Zone (Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D – a fixed, known list used across every project in the company) the activity belongs to, for consistent enterprise-wide grouping and filtering; and (2) a free-text field for the specific permit reference number tied to each individual activity, which is unique per activity and not a repeatable category.
question: Should the planner set up requirement (1) and requirement (2) as Activity Codes, User Defined Fields (UDFs), or does it not matter which is used for each?
expectedAnswer: Requirement (1) – Zone – should be an Activity Code: it is a fixed, reusable list of category values meant to be shared and consistently grouped/filtered/reported across activities (and potentially across projects if defined at EPS or Global level). Requirement (2) – permit reference number – should be a User Defined Field: it is unique, free-form data per activity rather than a value drawn from a repeatable pick list, which is exactly what UDFs are for.
strongAnswer: Notes that Activity Codes are defined once with a controlled value list (preventing inconsistent free-text entries like 'Zone A' vs 'zone a' vs 'ZoneA'), which matters for reliable grouping/filtering, whereas forcing the unique permit numbers into an Activity Code would require creating a new code value for every single activity, defeating the purpose of a shared classification list.
expertAnswer: Adds that Activity Code scope (Global/EPS/Project) should be considered for the Zone code – if Zone naming is standard company-wide, defining it at EPS or Global level avoids re-creating it per project – while the UDF only needs to be Project (or EPS) scoped since it's not meant to be a shared classification.
explanation: Activity Codes are enterprise-configurable pick lists of a fixed set of values, ideal for classification data that repeats across many activities and needs consistent grouping/filtering/reporting. UDFs are per-activity custom fields (text, number, date, etc.) intended for data that is specific/unique to that activity and doesn't need a controlled shared value list. Using the wrong tool for the wrong data either forces artificial 'one value per activity' codes (bloating the code value list) or loses the consistency benefits of a controlled list for genuinely categorical data.
reasoning: The distinguishing test is repeatability and control: if many activities should share the exact same value from a known, limited set, it's a code; if the value is essentially unique text/number data captured per activity, it's a UDF.
commonMistakes: Using a UDF for a value that should be standardized (like Zone), leading to inconsistent free-text entries across the team.
Trying to create a new Activity Code value for every unique permit number, bloating the enterprise code list unnecessarily.
redFlags: Cannot articulate any functional difference between codes and UDFs at all.

skill: Choosing the correct scope (Global, EPS, or Project) when defining a new Activity Code
scenario: A planning department runs P6 for a construction group with dozens of active projects across three regional divisions. They want a 'Trade' code (Concrete, Steel, MEP, Finishes, Earthworks) available and consistently valued the exact same way on every single project the company ever runs, including future ones, without each project's planner having to recreate it. Separately, one specific data center project needs a one-off 'Commissioning Stage' code (IST, IQ, OQ, PQ) that is meaningless to every other project type the company runs.
question: At what scope should the 'Trade' code and the 'Commissioning Stage' code each be defined, and why?
expectedAnswer: 'Trade' should be a Global Activity Code: Global codes are available to every project in the entire database automatically, which matches the requirement for consistent, company-wide reuse without recreating it per project. 'Commissioning Stage' should be a Project-level Activity Code, scoped only to that one data center project, since it is not relevant to other project types and doesn't need to be visible/selectable enterprise-wide.
strongAnswer: Notes that EPS-level codes sit between the two – available to all projects under a specific EPS node/branch – which would be the right choice if, say, only the data center division (not the whole company) needed 'Commissioning Stage' shared across multiple data center projects.
expertAnswer: Flags the governance trade-off: over-using Global codes for things that are really project- or division-specific clutters the enterprise code list for every planner in the company, while under-scoping (making everything Project-level) forces repetitive re-creation and risks inconsistent value naming across projects that should share a code.
explanation: P6 Activity Codes can be defined at three scopes: Global (every project in the database), EPS (every project under a chosen EPS node), or Project (only the current project). The correct scope choice depends on how broadly the classification needs to be shared/reused, balanced against not cluttering the enterprise list with narrow, project-specific values.

Defining Trade at Project level repeatedly across dozens of projects, risking inconsistent value spelling/order between projects.

skill: Knowing P6's default Duration Type and its basic effect
scenario: A junior planner creates a brand-new activity on a warehouse racking installation project and, without touching the Duration Type field at all, assigns one Installation Crew resource at 8h/d with Original Duration 4d. The site supervisor later asks the planner to add a second crew, expecting the duration to roughly halve, but it doesn't change at all.
question: What field should the planner check first to understand why the duration didn't change, and what is it most likely set to given the planner never touched it?
explanation: The planner should first check the activity's Duration Type field on the General tab. Since it was never manually changed, it is almost certainly still sitting at Fixed Units/Time – P6's default Duration Type for every new activity unless the project default or the activity itself is deliberately changed. Fixed Units/Time keeps each resource's Units/Time (rate) constant; adding a second crew at the same 8h/d rate does not by itself force Duration to shrink under this type, which explains why the supervisor's expectation of automatic compression wasn't met.
reasoning: P6 offers four Duration Types (Fixed Units/Time, Fixed Duration & Units/Time, Fixed Units, Fixed Duration & Units), each fixing a different pair of {Duration, Units, Units/Time} and letting the third vary; because Fixed Units/Time is applied automatically to new activities, an untouched activity's behavior when resources are added is governed by that default unless someone deliberately chose otherwise.
commonMistakes: Assuming Fixed Duration & Units/Time is the default because it is the most commonly discussed type in training materials.
Confusing Duration Type with Activity Type when diagnosing this symptom.
Assuming adding any resource always shortens duration regardless of Duration Type.
redFlags: Changes the Duration Type immediately without first confirming what it currently is, risking an unintended side effect on other resource assignments.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – Duration Type dropdown, to confirm the current setting.
Project Details > Defaults tab – Duration Type field, to confirm what new activities inherit by default.
Activity Details > Resources tab – observe what actually changed (likely total Units, not Duration) after the second crew was added.

skill: Recognizing that Fixed Duration & Units/Time prevents resourcing changes from compressing an activity's duration
scenario: On a manufacturing plant commissioning project, activity 'Functional Performance Test – Line 3' has Duration Type = Fixed Duration & Units/Time, Original Duration 5d, with one Commissioning Engineer assigned at 8h/d. The commissioning manager asks the planner to assign a second Commissioning Engineer to the same activity, expecting the test to now finish in half the time.
question: Will assigning a second engineer shorten this activity's 5-day duration? What actually changes?
explanation: No, the duration will not shorten. Under Fixed Duration & Units/Time, both the Duration (5d) and each resource's Units/Time (8h/d) are held constant by definition; adding a second engineer only adds another 8h/d resource working across the same fixed 5-day span, which doubles the total budgeted Units (labor-hours) rather than compressing the schedule. This is often the physically correct outcome for a scripted functional test that has a fixed test duration regardless of headcount (e.g., a system needs to run through its test sequence for a fixed number of days no matter how many engineers are watching it), so the real question for the commissioning manager is whether the test itself can actually be compressed at all – not a P6 configuration issue.
reasoning: Fixed Duration & Units/Time locks Duration and rate, leaving only total Units free to move when a resource assignment is edited, so it structurally cannot produce duration compression from adding resources.
commonMistakes: Assuming any added resource in P6 shortens duration by default.
Recommending a Duration Type change purely to make the number the manager wants appear, without checking whether the work is genuinely time-driven rather than effort-driven.
redFlags: Changes Duration Type just to produce a shorter number without evaluating whether the underlying test process can actually be compressed.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – confirm Duration Type = Fixed Duration & Units/Time.
Activity Details > Resources tab – observe Budgeted Units doubling after the second engineer is added, while Duration stays at 5d.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can name Fixed Units as the compression-capable type and reason about whether it's physically valid for a scripted test.

skill: Diagnosing why an activity under Fixed Units did not compress as much as expected when a resource was added
scenario: On a highway earthworks package, activity 'Compact Subgrade – Section 12' has Duration Type = Fixed Units, Original Duration 8d, with one Compaction Roller Crew assigned at 8h/d. The site engineer adds a second Compaction Roller Crew, also at 8h/d, expecting the duration to roughly halve to 4 days. After running F9, the duration only drops to 5 days.
question: Given Fixed Units effort-driven behavior, why might the duration compression be less than the naive 'double the crews, halve the duration' expectation?
explanation: Fixed Units keeps total budgeted Units (total labor/effort) constant and recalculates Duration as the combined resource rate changes, so in principle doubling the assigned rate should roughly halve Duration – but several real factors commonly prevent the full theoretical compression: the calendars of the two crews may not be identical (e.g., the second crew is on a calendar with fewer working hours per day or different working days), the activity may have a Duration Type at the resource-assignment level that isn't uniformly 'Driving' for both resources, one resource may be marked non-driving, or a physical/calendar constraint may be capping how early the activity can finish. Any of these would mean the two crews are not truly working at a simple additive combined rate across identical time, producing less compression than the naive halving assumption.
reasoning: The simple 'add a crew, halve the time' intuition assumes both resources share an identical calendar and both are actively driving the activity's duration at their full assigned rate for the same available working time; in practice compaction crews often differ in shift calendar, and P6's Fixed Units math is driven by whichever resource assignments are marked as driving the activity, not a naive averaging.
commonMistakes: Assuming Fixed Units always produces perfectly proportional compression regardless of calendar differences.
Not checking whether both resource assignments are actually flagged as 'Driving' the activity.
redFlags: Declares this a P6 calculation bug without checking calendars or driving-resource flags first.
p6Checks: Activity Details > Resources tab – compare each crew's assigned calendar (via the resource dictionary) for working days/hours differences.
Activity Details > Resources tab – check the 'Driving' flag/column for each resource assignment.
Confirm no constraint on the activity is capping the earliest possible finish.

skill: Distinguishing Physical, Duration, and Units percent complete types and their calculation basis
scenario: On an oil & gas EPC project, activity 'Fabricate and Deliver Pressure Vessel PV-204' (a long-lead procurement item) has Percent Complete Type = Duration. The site team reports the vendor has confirmed the vessel is genuinely 80% through fabrication based on the vendor's own progress photos and milestone certificate, but the planner has only updated Remaining Duration down slightly, so the activity's calculated % Complete shows just 20%.
question: Why does the activity show only 20% Complete despite the vendor confirming 80% physical progress, and what should the planner do to reflect reality accurately?
explanation: Under Percent Complete Type = Duration, P6 calculates % Complete purely from (Original Duration - Remaining Duration) / Original Duration – it has no awareness of the vendor's actual physical fabrication progress unless Remaining Duration is updated to match. Because the planner only trimmed Remaining Duration slightly, the duration-based math produces 20%, completely disconnected from the true 80% physical status. The correct fix is either to update Remaining Duration to a value consistent with 80% completion, or – better for a procurement item like this, where physical fabrication progress is the real driver rather than elapsed calendar time – switch the activity's Percent Complete Type to Physical, which allows the planner to directly enter the vendor-confirmed 80% independent of Remaining Duration.
reasoning: Each of P6's three Percent Complete Types uses a different calculation basis: Physical is a manually entered value (or driven by weighted Activity Steps) independent of duration/units; Duration is computed automatically from Remaining Duration; Units is computed automatically from Actual Units versus (Actual + Remaining) Units. Choosing the wrong type for the nature of the work (here, vendor-reported physical fabrication progress rather than elapsed working days) produces a % Complete that doesn't reflect reality.
commonMistakes: Assuming % Complete always reflects true physical progress regardless of which Percent Complete Type is set.
Trying to force the correct % by artificially manipulating Remaining Duration instead of using Physical % Complete for this kind of milestone-certified progress.
redFlags: Reports 20% up the chain to the client/PM without investigating why it disagrees with the vendor-confirmed 80%.
p6Checks: Activity Details > Status tab – Percent Complete Type field and current Physical/Duration/Units % values.
Activity Details > Status tab – Remaining Duration field, to see what's actually driving the Duration-based % shown.
Consider whether switching to Physical % (with a manually entered or Steps-driven value) better represents procurement/fabrication milestone progress going forward.

skill: Evaluating the consequences of switching an activity's Percent Complete Type after progress has already been recorded
scenario: Six months into a rail signalling project, a senior planner discovers that 40 in-progress activities were set up with Percent Complete Type = Duration, but the site team has actually been reporting progress based on physical inspection milestones (cable pulled, terminated, tested) that don't correlate well with elapsed working days. The planner is considering bulk-switching all 40 activities to Physical Percent Complete Type immediately, mid-reporting-period, to better reflect reality going forward.
question: What should the planner do next, and what are the risks of switching Percent Complete Type on already-progressed activities without careful handling?
explanation: Switching Percent Complete Type on an activity that already has recorded Remaining Duration, Actual Duration, and history is not purely cosmetic – it changes how future % Complete is calculated and can cause a visible, unexplained jump or drop in the reported % the moment the switch is made (since Physical % must now be manually entered or steps-driven, and won't automatically match whatever the Duration-based % happened to show). Before bulk-switching, the planner should: (1) determine the correct current Physical % for each of the 40 activities from the actual site inspection records so the entered values are defensible, not guessed; (2) communicate the change to whoever consumes progress reports (PM, client, EVM team) so a sudden jump in reported % Complete on the next update is understood as a data-quality correction, not a schedule change; (3) consider whether this should be done at a clean period boundary (right after a status update, before the next one starts) rather than mid-period, to avoid confusing that period's earned-progress comparison; and (4) update the activities' default Percent Complete Type going forward (and ideally the project default for future similar activities) so the same 40-activity problem doesn't recur on the next batch of work.
reasoning: Percent Complete Type is a configuration choice about how % is calculated, not a passive label; changing it after real progress exists can silently redefine what 'percent complete' means for an activity that already has a reporting history, with downstream effects on any Earned Value or S-curve reporting that consumes that % Complete value. A senior planner needs to manage this as a controlled data-quality correction, not a quiet field-level edit.
commonMistakes: Treating the switch as purely technical/cosmetic with no need to inform stakeholders.
Guessing Physical % values instead of grounding them in actual inspection records.
Making the change mid-period, muddying that period's progress comparison.
redFlags: Bulk-switches the type and enters Physical % values without any documented basis, risking a defensible audit trail gap if progress is later challenged (e.g., by the client or in a claim).

Project Details > Defaults tab – whether the project default Percent Complete Type should also be corrected for future activities.
Global Change (Tools > Global Change, Professional) could be considered to bulk-apply the type change efficiently across the 40 activities, provided the correct Physical % source data is ready first.

skill: Knowing what to verify before running the schedule calculation at a period-end update
scenario: It is the last working day of the reporting period on a warehouse construction project. The planner has just finished entering all actual progress (Actual Start/Finish dates, Remaining Durations, and Physical % updates) reported by site supervisors, and is about to press F9 to run the schedule for the monthly update.
question: What should the planner check first, immediately before running F9, to make sure the update calculates correctly?
explanation: Before running F9, the planner should verify the Data Date has been advanced to the correct period-end date (it drives where P6 draws the line between actual/historical work and remaining/future work). They should also confirm all reported actuals have actually been entered for the period (no activities were missed), and check that no activity shows an Actual Start after the new Data Date or a Remaining Duration greater than zero on something marked 100% complete, since these inconsistencies produce misleading results once scheduled. Only after Data Date is correctly set and the update data is complete should F9 be run.
reasoning: The Data Date is the pivot point P6 uses to separate what already happened (actuals) from what is still to be forecast (remaining work); if it is left at the previous period's date, the schedule will recalculate remaining work from the wrong starting point, producing an inaccurate forecast even though the actual progress entries themselves are correct.
commonMistakes: Running F9 without first advancing the Data Date, then wondering why forecast dates look wrong.
Assuming F9 itself will 'know' the current reporting date automatically.
redFlags: Runs the schedule reflexively without checking Data Date at all as a matter of habit.
p6Checks: Schedule dialog (F9) – Data Date field at the top, confirm it matches the intended period-end date before clicking Schedule.
Activities view – scan for activities with Actual Start after the intended new Data Date, or 100% Complete activities still showing Remaining Duration > 0.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can predict the downstream symptom, not just recite the check.

skill: Diagnosing a stale schedule update caused by an un-advanced Data Date
scenario: On a solar farm construction project, the planner enters this month's actual progress (mid-March) and runs F9, but forgets to advance the Data Date, which is still sitting at the prior update (mid-February). After scheduling, several activities the site confirmed as started in early March still show Remaining Duration calculated as if no time had passed since mid-February, and the reported project forecast finish barely moved.
question: What is the underlying cause of this stale-looking update, and how should the planner fix it?
explanation: Because the Data Date was never advanced, P6 recalculated remaining work as if the current 'as of' point in time was still mid-February, effectively ignoring the month of actual progress that just occurred for forecasting purposes – even though the Actual Start/Finish and % Complete entries themselves were correctly recorded. The fix is to open the Schedule (F9) dialog, set the Data Date to the correct mid-March period-end date, and re-run the schedule; this repositions the forward pass starting point so remaining durations are recalculated from the true current status date.
reasoning: The Data Date, not the mere presence of Actual dates, is what tells P6 where 'now' is for scheduling remaining work; actual progress entries record what happened, but the Data Date determines from where P6 projects what happens next.
commonMistakes: Assuming entering Actual Start/Finish dates alone is sufficient to move the schedule forward.
Blaming relationship logic or calendars for a stale-looking forecast before checking Data Date.
redFlags: Starts re-checking or rebuilding relationship logic before confirming the Data Date was correctly advanced.
p6Checks: Schedule dialog (F9) – confirm the Data Date field shows the correct current period date, not the prior period's.
Project Details > Dates tab also displays the current Data Date for the project.
After correcting Data Date and re-scheduling, verify Remaining Duration and forecast dates update sensibly for the newly progressed activities.

skill: Distinguishing Data Date from Current Date
question: What is the difference between the schedule's 'Data Date' and the 'Current Date' shown in P6?

options.label: A
options.text: Data Date is the status/as-of date the planner sets for the schedule calculation (separating actuals from remaining work); Current Date reflects today's real calendar date on the computer running P6

options.label: B
options.text: They are two names for exactly the same field and always show the same date

options.label: C
options.text: Data Date is set once at project creation and never changes; Current Date is updated every schedule run

options.label: D
options.text: Current Date determines which activities are marked critical; Data Date has no effect on calculations

explanation: The Data Date is a planner-controlled field representing the 'as of' status point for the schedule – it drives which work is treated as actual/historical versus remaining/forecast during the F9 calculation. The Current Date is simply today's real-world date as read from the system clock, used for display purposes (e.g., a 'Today' vertical line on the Gantt chart) and is not itself an input to the CPM calculation.
reasoning: Data Date must be deliberately advanced each period by the planner to reflect the actual reporting cut-off, and can legitimately differ from today's real calendar date (e.g., a monthly update might be run a few days after the true period-end Data Date it represents).
commonMistakes: Assuming Data Date automatically tracks today's date without manual updating.
Believing Current Date affects float or critical path calculations.

Gantt Chart – the 'Today' vertical marker line, driven by Current Date, distinct from the Data Date line.

skill: Diagnosing a layout visibility problem caused by Personal versus Global (shared) save scope
scenario: A planner builds a detailed progress-tracking layout (specific columns, grouping by WBS and Activity Code, a custom filter for 'Behind Schedule' activities) for a shipbuilding project and saves it. The project manager, logging into the same P6 database on a different workstation, reports they cannot find that layout in their Layout list at all.
question: What is the most likely reason the PM cannot see the layout, and how should the planner fix it?
explanation: The most likely reason is that the layout was saved with scope 'Personal' rather than 'Global' (or, in EPPM, 'Everyone'/shared) – a Personal layout is only visible to the specific user account that created it and does not appear for any other user, including the PM logging in from another workstation. The fix is for the planner to re-save (or edit the save scope of) the layout and choose the Global/shared option instead of Personal, after which it becomes available to other users of the same database.
reasoning: P6 layouts have a save-scope setting specifically to control whether a layout is a private convenience for one user or a standardized shared view for the team; this is a very common source of 'I built it but nobody else can see it' confusion for new planners.
commonMistakes: Assuming all saved layouts are automatically visible to everyone with database access.
Re-creating the entire layout from scratch for the PM instead of simply changing its save scope.

Confirm the PM's own Layout list refreshes to show the layout once it is saved/re-saved as Global.

skill: Diagnosing an empty filter result caused by incorrect AND/OR (All/Any) logic
scenario: A planner on a hospital expansion project builds a custom filter intending to show all activities that are either behind schedule (Total Float < 0) or belong to the Structural discipline. They add two parameters – 'Total Float is less than 0' and 'Activity Code Discipline equals Structural' – but set the filter to combine conditions using 'All of the following' (AND) instead of 'Any of the following' (OR). When applied, the Activities view shows zero activities, even though the planner knows there are both late structural activities and late non-structural activities in the schedule.
question: Why does the filter return no results, and what should be changed to get the intended outcome?
explanation: With 'All of the following' (AND) logic, P6 only shows activities that satisfy both conditions simultaneously – Total Float < 0 AND Discipline = Structural at the same time. If, in this particular dataset, none of the currently late activities happen to be Structural (or none of the Structural activities happen to be late right now), the AND combination legitimately returns zero rows even though each condition individually has matches. The planner's actual intent – late OR Structural – requires switching the filter's logic to 'Any of the following' (OR), which shows an activity if it satisfies either condition.
reasoning: Filter logic type (All/AND vs Any/OR) fundamentally changes what a multi-parameter filter returns; a common authoring mistake is picking AND when the intended meaning was really OR (or vice versa), producing either an unexpectedly empty or unexpectedly broad result set.
commonMistakes: Assuming a filter returning zero results always means there's no data matching the general intent, rather than checking the AND/OR logic first.
Not realizing multiple parameters in one filter default to a single combination mode covering all of them.
redFlags: Concludes the schedule has no late or Structural activities at all, rather than questioning the filter logic.
p6Checks: Filters dialog (View > Filters or Filter toolbar) – check the 'Show activities that match: All of the following / Any of the following' setting at the top of the filter's parameter list.
Test each parameter individually as a single-condition filter to confirm each independently returns results before combining them.

followUpQuestions.prompt: How would you build a filter for 'Structural activities that are also late', as opposed to 'late OR Structural'?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate understands when AND is actually the correct choice, reinforcing they're not just memorizing 'always use OR'.

question: How should the planner configure Group and Sort to produce this view, and what P6 feature displays the rolled-up totals per band?

P6 automatically displays a summary band row for each group/subgroup combination; adding the Original Duration and Budgeted Cost columns to the layout causes those band rows to show rolled-up totals (sum, depending on the field) for all activities within that WBS/Discipline combination, giving exactly the structured rollup the PM asked for.

skill: Recognizing that Total Float and other calculated columns are blank until the schedule has been run at least once
scenario: A junior planner imports a brand-new XER schedule for a logistics warehouse project into P6, adds the Total Float and Free Float columns to the Activities view, but every single activity shows a blank value in both columns instead of numbers.
question: What is the most likely reason both float columns are blank, and what single action will most likely resolve it?
explanation: Total Float and Free Float are calculated results of the CPM forward and backward pass, not stored input data – if the schedule has not yet been calculated in this P6 session/database (or the import did not carry forward previously calculated values in a way P6 trusts as current), those columns will show blank until F9 is run. The fix is simply to run the schedule (F9) once; after scheduling completes, both float columns should populate with calculated values for every activity.
reasoning: P6 only populates float, early/late dates, and criticality after executing the scheduling algorithm; a freshly imported or newly built set of activities and relationships has no calculated float data sitting in those fields until that calculation actually runs.
commonMistakes: Assuming a blank float column means a data corruption or import error rather than simply an un-scheduled project.
Trying to manually type float values into the column instead of running F9.
redFlags: Attempts to manually enter float values, which are read-only calculated fields and cannot be typed in directly.
p6Checks: Run Tools > Schedule (F9) once, then re-check the Total Float and Free Float columns.
Activities view – confirm Early/Late Start/Finish columns are also populated after scheduling, confirming the calculation ran.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate distinguishes 'never scheduled' from 'scheduled but logic-incomplete', a related but different root cause.

skill: Distinguishing Admin Preferences, Project Defaults, and User Preferences by scope
scenario: A new planner joins a company using P6 Professional and wants to change three things: (1) the date format shown throughout their own screen from DD-MM-YY to DD-MMM-YY, without affecting how dates look for any other user; (2) the default Duration Type applied to every new activity created on the specific EPC project they're assigned to; (3) the company-wide standard 'Hours per Day' conversion (e.g., 8 hours = 1 day) used across every project in the database.
question: Which P6 settings area – User Preferences, Project Details > Defaults, or Admin Preferences – controls each of these three requirements?
expectedAnswer: (1) is controlled by User Preferences – a per-user, client-side setting (Dates tab) that affects only how that individual's own session displays dates, with no effect on other users or on stored data. (2) is controlled by Project Details > Defaults tab – a per-project setting that determines the Duration Type (and other defaults) applied automatically to new activities created within that one project. (3) is controlled by Admin Preferences (Time Periods tab) – a database-wide setting shared by every project and every user in that P6 installation.
strongAnswer: Notes the general pattern: User Preferences = personal display only, no data impact; Project Defaults = scoped to one project's new-activity behavior; Admin Preferences = global, database-wide conversions/settings that affect calculations and displays for everyone.
expertAnswer: Adds that changing Admin Preferences (like Hours per Day) is a higher-risk, organization-wide action that can shift how existing budgeted Units/durations are interpreted or displayed across every active project, so it typically requires administrator-level authorization and careful communication, unlike a purely personal User Preferences change.
explanation: P6 settings are intentionally split by scope: User Preferences are personal and client-side (display only), Project Defaults are per-project (affecting only new activities in that project going forward), and Admin Preferences are database-wide (affecting every project and user). Picking the wrong scope either fails to achieve the intended change or unintentionally affects far more than intended.
reasoning: Understanding these three scopes correctly prevents both under-reach (trying to fix something globally via a personal setting) and over-reach (accidentally changing a database-wide setting when only a personal or project-specific change was needed).
commonMistakes: Trying to change the date format via Project Defaults or Admin Preferences instead of the correct personal User Preferences setting.
Assuming a Project Defaults change retroactively affects existing activities in that project.
Not realizing an Admin Preferences change is shared across every project and user in the database.
redFlags: Recommends changing Admin Preferences to solve a purely personal display preference, risking unintended company-wide impact.
p6Checks: Edit > User Preferences > Dates tab (personal date format).
Project Details > Defaults tab (per-project Duration Type default).
Admin > Admin Preferences > Time Periods tab (database-wide Hours per Day/Week/Month/Year).

skill: Using weighted Activity Steps to drive automatic Physical Percent Complete
scenario: On a substation electrical works project, activity 'Install and Test LV Switchgear Panel' has Percent Complete Type = Physical, and the User Preferences Calculations tab has 'Activity percent complete based on activity steps' enabled. The planner defines four Steps under the activity's Steps tab: Deliver Panel (weight 1), Install & Terminate (weight 3), Energize (weight 2), and Function Test & Sign-off (weight 4), for a total weight of 10. The site marks 'Deliver Panel' and 'Install & Terminate' as complete.
question: What Physical Percent Complete will P6 automatically calculate for this activity, and how is that number derived?
explanation: With Steps-based percent complete enabled, Physical % Complete is calculated as the sum of the weights of completed Steps divided by the total weight of all Steps, expressed as a percentage. Here, the completed steps are Deliver Panel (weight 1) and Install & Terminate (weight 3), totaling 4 out of a total weight of 10 (1+3+2+4), giving 4/10 = 40%.
reasoning: Weighted Activity Steps let a planner represent uneven progress milestones within a single activity (some steps represent more of the real effort/value than others) instead of assuming every step counts equally; P6 automatically rolls this up into Physical % Complete whenever the Steps-based calculation option is enabled, removing the need to manually estimate a percentage.
commonMistakes: Assuming each completed step counts as an equal 25% regardless of its assigned weight (which would incorrectly give 50% here by counting 2 of 4 steps as complete).
Forgetting that this feature only drives % Complete automatically when the 'based on activity steps' preference is actually enabled.
p6Checks: Edit > User Preferences > Calculations tab – confirm 'Activity percent complete based on activity steps' is checked.
Activity Details > Steps tab – review each step's weight and completion checkbox.
Activity Details > Status tab – confirm Percent Complete Type = Physical and observe the calculated % matches the weighted step completion.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the planner later adds a fifth Step after some progress has already been recorded, what happens to the calculated Physical %?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that the calculation recalculates dynamically against whatever the current total weight is.

skill: Locating where Primary and Secondary constraints are applied to an activity
scenario: A client's contract requires that activity 'Handover Building Permit Submission' must not be submitted before a specific regulatory date, and separately must not slip past a second, later drop-dead date under any circumstances. A planner new to P6 isn't sure whether this needs one constraint or two, or where to enter them.
question: Can P6 represent both a not-before date and a not-after date on the same activity, and where would the planner set this up?
expectedAnswer: Yes. The planner should use Activity Details > Status tab, where an activity can carry both a Primary Constraint and a Secondary Constraint simultaneously, each with its own type and date. A 'Start On or After' (or similar) constraint set to the regulatory not-before date, combined with a 'Finish On or Before' (or a Mandatory Finish, depending on how strictly it must be enforced) constraint set to the drop-dead date, together bound the activity within that required window.
strongAnswer: Notes the practical distinction between the softer 'On or Before/After' constraints (which still allow the schedule logic to move the date earlier/later within the bound) versus a Mandatory constraint (which forces the exact date regardless of logic), and recommends choosing based on how strictly the drop-dead date must be enforced.
expertAnswer: Cautions that stacking two constraints on one activity should be used sparingly and documented clearly (e.g., in the Notebook), since constrained activities are a common source of schedule quality findings in an independent review, and an unexplained dual constraint can look like a data-entry artifact rather than a deliberate contractual requirement if not annotated.
explanation: Constraints are applied on the Status tab of Activity Details, where a planner selects a Primary Constraint type and date, and can also set a Secondary Constraint with its own type and date – both apply simultaneously to bound the activity's calculated dates from two directions at once, exactly matching a 'not before X, not after Y' contractual requirement.
reasoning: P6 keeps constraint assignment as structured, calculated-impact fields (not free text or codes) because constraints directly participate in the forward/backward pass date calculation, unlike Activity Codes or Notebook entries which are purely descriptive/classification data with no scheduling effect.
commonMistakes: Assuming only one constraint (Primary) can ever be applied per activity, and that a two-sided date window isn't possible.
Confusing constraints with Activity Codes or Notebook topics, which have no effect on CPM calculation.
redFlags: Attempts to represent the two-sided requirement using two separate milestone activities and a Notebook note instead of using the Primary/Secondary constraint fields that exist for exactly this purpose.
p6Checks: Activity Details > Status tab – Primary Constraint and Secondary Constraint dropdowns and date fields.
Notebook tab – document the contractual reason for the constraints so a later reviewer understands why they're there.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is the practical difference between a 'Finish On or Before' constraint and a 'Mandatory Finish' constraint for the drop-dead date?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of constraint strictness and its effect on schedule logic.

skill: Deciding when to use Global Change for mass edits and managing its risk
scenario: A planning manager needs to reassign the Calendar field from 'Standard 5-Day Workweek' to 'Standard 6-Day Workweek' on roughly 650 activities across a large refinery turnaround schedule (every activity whose Activity Code 'Work Area' = 'Unit 4'), ahead of an accelerated recovery plan. One planner suggests filtering to those 650 activities and manually changing the Calendar field on each one; another suggests using Global Change to apply the reassignment in one operation.
question: Which approach should the planning manager choose, and what precautions should be taken before executing it on 650 activities?
expectedAnswer: Global Change is the correct tool for a mass, rule-based edit like this – it can apply a formula (IF Work Area = Unit 4 THEN set Calendar = Standard 6-Day Workweek) across all matching activities in a single controlled operation, far faster and less error-prone than 650 manual edits. Before executing it, the manager should take a project backup (or work in a copy of the project) so the change can be reverted if something is wrong, use Global Change's Preview/Report feature to review exactly which activities and values will change before committing, and run F9 afterward to confirm the recalculated dates make sense.
strongAnswer: Notes that Global Change changes are not easily undone with a simple 'undo' once committed and saved, which is precisely why the backup and preview step are not optional extras but a required part of using the tool safely at this scale.
expertAnswer: Adds that reassigning 650 activities' calendars will shift remaining durations and dates for all of them simultaneously on the next schedule run, so the manager should also assess the downstream ripple effect on the critical path and any resource leveling before/after, and communicate the change to the team so a large, sudden date shift isn't mistaken for a scheduling error.
explanation: Global Change (Tools > Global Change in P6 Professional) is purpose-built for exactly this kind of rule-based, mass-edit scenario, letting the manager apply an IF/THEN formula against a filtered or coded subset of activities instead of editing each one by hand. Because it operates on hundreds of activities at once and its effects are not trivially reversible, it should always be preceded by a backup and a preview/report step, not applied blind.
reasoning: Manual editing of 650 activities is slow and highly error-prone (missed activities, inconsistent values); Global Change is designed for exactly this use case, but its power is also its risk – an incorrect formula or filter can silently apply an unwanted change to hundreds of activities at once, so professional practice treats it as a controlled operation requiring backup and verification.
commonMistakes: Manually editing hundreds of activities one by one when Global Change exists precisely to avoid this.
Running Global Change directly on the live/only copy of the schedule without a backup or preview step.
redFlags: Applies Global Change directly to the production schedule with no backup and no preview of affected activities, especially at this scale.
p6Checks: Tools > Global Change – build a formula: IF Activity Code 'Work Area' = 'Unit 4' THEN Calendar = Standard 6-Day Workweek.
Use the Global Change Report/Preview option before clicking Commit Changes.
Take a project backup (Export/Copy) beforehand; re-run F9 and review the schedule after applying.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate would refine the filter/formula rather than proceeding and manually correcting afterward.

skill: Applying the Total Float threshold setting that defines 'critical' in Schedule Options
scenario: In the Schedule Options dialog (accessed via the F9 Schedule dialog's Options button), 'Define critical activities as Total Float less than or equal to' is set to 3 days. After scheduling, an activity called 'Procure Structural Steel' shows a Total Float of exactly 3 days.
question: Based only on this Total Float threshold setting, will P6 flag 'Procure Structural Steel' (Total Float = 3d) as critical? Answer Yes (1) or No (0), and state the boundary rule being applied.
explanation: Yes. The setting uses 'less than or equal to', so an activity with Total Float exactly equal to the threshold value (3 days) is included as critical, not excluded. Only an activity with Total Float greater than 3 days would fall outside the critical definition under this setting.
reasoning: This threshold is a configurable definition of 'critical' independent of the strict CPM convention of Total Float = 0; many projects widen the definition (e.g., to 3, 5, or 10 days) to also flag near-critical activities for closer management attention, and the boundary is inclusive because the operator is 'less than or equal to', not 'less than'.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'critical' in P6 always strictly means Total Float = 0, without checking whether the project's Schedule Options threshold has been widened.
Misreading 'less than or equal to' as excluding the boundary value.
p6Checks: Schedule dialog (F9) > Options button > General tab (or equivalent) – 'Define critical activities as Total Float less than or equal to ___ days' field.
Activities view – apply the built-in 'Critical' filter or check the Critical column/flag after scheduling to confirm which activities are flagged.
