skill: Choosing between the Total Float threshold and the Longest Path method for defining critical activities when negative float is present
scenario: On a delayed metro station project, the schedule currently carries an imposed Finish constraint, and after the latest update, dozens of activities across multiple paths show negative Total Float ranging from -2 to -40 days, because they all fall behind the constrained finish date to varying degrees. Using the standard 'Total Float <= 0' definition, the Critical filter now highlights a very large, sprawling set of activities across the schedule, making it hard for the team to see the single true driving chain to project completion.
question: What alternative approach is available in P6's Schedule Options to better isolate the true driving path in this situation, and why would it help here?
expectedAnswer: Switch the critical activity definition in Schedule Options from the Total Float threshold to 'Longest Path'. The Longest Path method identifies critical activities as those on the single longest continuous chain of driving relationships back from the project (or constrained) finish, regardless of their individual Total Float value, rather than flagging every activity whose float happens to fall below a threshold. In a multi-constraint, negative-float situation like this, many unrelated paths can all show negative float simultaneously (because each is behind its own governing constraint), which floods the Total Float-based critical filter with activities that aren't actually all on the one true driving chain – Longest Path cuts through that noise to show the actual sequence of activities directly determining the project's finish date.
strongAnswer: Notes that Longest Path and Total Float-based critical definitions can genuinely disagree in multi-path, multi-constraint schedules, and that a planner should understand both rather than treating 'critical' as a single universal concept.
expertAnswer: Adds that neither definition should be blindly trusted alone in a heavily constrained, negative-float schedule – the planner should also sanity-check the constraints themselves (are they still valid/necessary) since an unnecessary or stale constraint can be the actual reason so many paths show negative float, rather than genuine schedule slippage.
explanation: P6's Schedule Options offers two distinct ways to define 'critical': a Total Float threshold (simple, but can over- or under-flag activities when many paths are constrained independently) and Longest Path (identifies the actual continuous driving chain to the finish). In a sprawling negative-float situation with an imposed constraint, Longest Path is generally the better tool for isolating the true driver of the project finish date.
reasoning: Total Float is calculated per path relative to whatever constrains that path; when multiple paths each have their own negative float relative to different or the same constraint, a simple threshold flags all of them as 'critical' even though only one continuous chain is actually determining the overall project finish – Longest Path traces that specific chain instead of flagging by float value alone.
commonMistakes: Assuming Total Float <= 0 always identifies exactly one clean critical path.
Not knowing Longest Path exists as an alternative, configurable definition in Schedule Options.
redFlags: Recommends manually and subjectively picking which negative-float activities 'look' critical instead of using the Longest Path calculation option.
p6Checks: Schedule dialog (F9) > Options – switch 'Define critical activities as' from the Total Float threshold to 'Longest Path'.
Re-run F9 and compare the set of activities flagged critical under each method.
Review whether the imposed Finish constraint driving the negative float is still valid/intended.

skill: Knowing P6's default out-of-sequence progress handling method
question: True or False: Retained Logic is P6's default method for handling out-of-sequence progress in the Schedule Options.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: True. Retained Logic is the default out-of-sequence progress option in P6's Schedule Options. It means that when a successor activity has progressed out of sequence (started before its predecessor logically finished), P6 still respects the predecessor's remaining relationship logic for scheduling any remaining (unprogressed) portion of the successor, rather than ignoring the relationship. The alternative option, Progress Override, instead lets the remaining work be scheduled as if the relationship no longer constrains it, treating it more like an unconstrained continuation.
reasoning: Out-of-sequence progress happens constantly on real projects (site conditions force starting a successor before its predecessor is technically finished); P6 needs a rule for how to treat the remaining portion of that successor going forward, and Retained Logic is the more conservative default, keeping the original relationship's constraint alive for the unprogressed work.
commonMistakes: Assuming Progress Override is the default because it 'sounds' like the more commonly discussed option in troubleshooting scenarios.
Confusing this setting with the Duration Type or Percent Complete Type settings.
p6Checks: Schedule dialog (F9) > Options – 'Out of Sequence Progress' setting, confirm current selection (Retained Logic vs Progress Override).

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate can connect the setting to an observable scheduling outcome.

skill: Deciding between a WBS Summary rollup view and a Project-level filtered report for executive reporting
scenario: A project controls lead needs to give an executive steering committee a single-bar-per-package view of a data center campus build (Building 1, Building 2, Substation, Site Infrastructure), each bar showing the overall Start/Finish envelope of everything underneath it, refreshed automatically every time the detailed schedule updates.
question: Should the lead build this using WBS Summary activities placed at each top WBS level, or by filtering/grouping the detailed activities in a report without adding WBS Summary activities? Justify the choice.
expectedAnswer: WBS Summary activities are the better fit here: once placed at the WBS level for each package (Building 1, Building 2, Substation, Site Infrastructure), P6 automatically recalculates each one's Start/Finish envelope to match its underlying detail activities on every schedule run, giving exactly the self-refreshing single-bar-per-package view requested with no manual maintenance. A filtered/grouped report can show the same information as summarized band rows, but that's a reporting-layer view built fresh each time from a filter/group configuration rather than a persistent schedule object – for a recurring, always-current executive bar chart, embedding WBS Summary activities directly in the schedule is generally more robust and directly usable in the Gantt/bar chart itself.
strongAnswer: Notes the trade-off: WBS Summary activities add extra rows to the schedule that need to be understood as non-scheduled rollups by anyone browsing the full activity list (and must not be mistaken for real work), whereas a Group and Sort banded view achieves a similar visual rollup without adding activities to the underlying network at all.
expertAnswer: Adds that for a formal steering-committee deliverable, many practitioners actually prefer a separate, purpose-built layout using Group and Sort banding (grouped by WBS with rollup columns) rather than adding WBS Summary activities into the working schedule, specifically to keep the live network free of non-CPM rollup objects that could be mistaken for schedulable activities by less experienced users; the right choice depends on whether the audience needs an actual Gantt bar per package (favoring WBS Summary) or a tabular rollup with totals (favoring Group and Sort).
explanation: Both WBS Summary activities and grouped/banded reporting views can produce a package-level rollup, but they operate differently: WBS Summary activities are real schedule objects living inside the network (automatically computed bars, refreshed with each schedule run) while Group and Sort banding is a layout-level presentation of the existing detail activities with no new objects added. Either is defensible; the decision depends on whether a literal rollup bar embedded in the network, or a clean banded report view, better serves the audience.
reasoning: The two approaches solve the same visual need through different mechanisms – one adds computed activities to the schedule itself, the other reshapes how existing activities are displayed – and a senior planner should be able to weigh the maintenance/clutter trade-offs of each rather than reflexively picking one.
commonMistakes: Assuming there is only one correct way to produce a package-level rollup view.
Not considering that WBS Summary activities become permanent objects in the schedule network.

skill: Knowing the basic workflow for customizing displayed columns in the Activities view

question: Is creating a UDF the right approach, and what is the most likely reason Free Float isn't already showing in the table?

Believing WBS structure changes affect which columns are visible.

skill: Identifying what to verify before running the first schedule calculation on a newly merged/imported schedule
scenario: A senior planner has just merged three subcontractor XER schedules (Civil, MEP, Facade) into one integrated master schedule for a mixed-use tower, ready to run the very first combined F9 schedule calculation before issuing it as the project's baseline.
question: Before running that first combined F9, what should the planner check to avoid issuing a baseline built on hidden defects?
explanation: Before the first combined schedule run, the planner should check: (1) Activity ID conflicts/duplicates between the three source schedules, now that they share one project; (2) open ends – activities with no predecessor and/or no successor introduced either within each subcontractor's own logic or, more importantly, at the interface points between the three schedules (the cross-schedule tie-in relationships that make this an integrated schedule rather than three parallel ones); (3) calendar consistency – whether each subcontractor schedule brought in its own set of calendars (possibly with different names/definitions for what should be the same working pattern) that now need to be reconciled or consolidated rather than left as three parallel, potentially inconsistent calendar sets; and (4) Activity Type and Duration Type defaults, since each subcontractor's schedule may have been built with different project-level defaults that are now inconsistent within a single integrated project. Only after these are reviewed (and interface relationships between the three disciplines are actually added, since merging files does not create logic links between them automatically) should the first schedule run be treated as trustworthy enough to baseline.
reasoning: Merging schedules from independent sources combines the data but does not automatically reconcile IDs, create missing interface logic between the sources, or harmonize calendars – any of these left unchecked will silently distort the very first combined critical path calculation, which then becomes the baseline everyone measures against for the rest of the project.
commonMistakes: Assuming a successful merge (no import errors) means the combined logic is sound.
Running F9 and baselining immediately without checking for missing interface relationships between the three subcontractor schedules.
Not checking whether calendar definitions actually match across the three source files even when calendar names look similar.
redFlags: Issues the merged schedule as baseline without any schedule health check (open ends, dangling logic, calendar review) purely because the import completed without error messages.
p6Checks: Filter for activities with no predecessor or no successor (open ends) across the whole integrated schedule.
Enterprise > Calendars – review all calendars now present in the project for duplicates/inconsistent definitions from the three sources.
Confirm cross-discipline interface relationships (e.g., Facade activities tied to Civil/Structural completion) actually exist – merging files alone does not create these links.
Check Activity ID uniqueness now that all three sets share one project.

skill: Choosing between Task Dependent and Resource Dependent activity types based on how resourcing should drive the schedule
scenario: On a district cooling plant project, activity 'Chiller Skid Commissioning' will have three specialist resources assigned who genuinely work independently and on different personal calendars: a Vendor Commissioning Engineer (client-approved 5-day calendar), an in-house Controls Technician (6-day calendar), and a third-party Vibration Analyst who is only available two specific days total. The planner wants the activity's overall duration to naturally reflect whichever of these three specialists actually takes the longest to finish their portion, rather than being tied to one fixed activity calendar.
question: Should this activity be set up as Task Dependent or Resource Dependent, and why?
expectedAnswer: Resource Dependent is the correct choice. Under Resource Dependent, each assigned resource's dates are driven by that resource's own individual calendar rather than a single fixed Activity Calendar, and the overall activity duration naturally extends to cover whichever resource takes longest to complete their assigned Units – exactly matching the requirement that the activity reflect the slowest of the three independently-calendared specialists.
strongAnswer: Notes that Task Dependent would instead force all three resources' work to be measured against one single activity calendar regardless of their real individual availability, which would misrepresent the Vibration Analyst's very limited two-day availability and could produce a duration that doesn't reflect reality.
expertAnswer: Adds a caution: Resource Dependent activities require every assigned resource to actually have an accurate, well-maintained individual calendar in the resource dictionary for this to work correctly – if the Vibration Analyst's two-day availability isn't correctly modeled as their resource calendar (e.g., using calendar exceptions to mark only those two specific days as working), Resource Dependent won't produce the intended result either, so the activity type choice alone isn't sufficient without correct underlying calendar data.
explanation: Task Dependent activities are governed by a single assigned Activity Calendar regardless of which resources are assigned, making them the wrong fit when different resources genuinely work to different personal calendars and the activity's real duration should reflect the slowest of them. Resource Dependent activities instead let each resource assignment be driven by that resource's own calendar, with the overall activity spanning until the last resource finishes – exactly the mechanic this scenario needs.
reasoning: The decision hinges on whether all assigned resources effectively share one working pattern (favoring Task Dependent, the simpler and more common default) or genuinely work to different independent calendars where the true duration should be resource-driven (favoring Resource Dependent) – this scenario explicitly describes the latter.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to Task Dependent because it's the more familiar/common activity type without evaluating whether the resourcing situation actually calls for Resource Dependent.
Choosing Resource Dependent without also verifying each resource's individual calendar is correctly configured to actually reflect their real availability.
redFlags: Recommends Resource Dependent purely because it 'sounds resource-related' without connecting it to the actual mechanical difference from Task Dependent.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – set Activity Type = Resource Dependent.
Enterprise > Resources – verify each of the three resources' individual calendar (including exceptions for the Vibration Analyst's limited two-day availability) is correctly configured.
After scheduling, check the Resources tab to confirm which resource is actually driving the activity's overall finish.

skill: Understanding Activity ID uniqueness scope (per project, not per database)
question: True or False: An Activity ID must be unique within its own project, but the same Activity ID (e.g., A1000) can exist in a different project in the same P6 database without conflict.

options.label: True
options.text: True

options.label: False
options.text: False

explanation: True. P6 only enforces Activity ID uniqueness within a single project. Two entirely separate projects in the same database can both legitimately contain an activity called A1000 with no conflict, because P6 tracks activities internally by a unique object ID, not by the visible Activity ID text alone. A conflict only arises if activities with duplicate IDs end up combined into the same project (for example, through a merge or import).
reasoning: This is exactly why merging or integrating multiple independently-built project schedules (each often starting from the same default A1000, A1010… numbering) frequently surfaces duplicate ID conflicts that didn't exist while the schedules were separate projects.

skill: Diagnosing an unexpected duration change traced to the activity's Duration Type when a resource assignment was edited
scenario: On a pipeline welding spread, activity 'Weld and NDT Test – Spread 6, Joint 214-260' was originally set up correctly with Duration Type = Fixed Duration & Units/Time, Original Duration 6d, one Welding Crew at 8h/d. Mid-project, a resource coordinator – without consulting the planner – simply increased the crew's assigned Units/Time from 8h/d to 12h/d directly on the resource assignment (to reflect authorized overtime), expecting only the total budgeted hours to increase. After the next F9, the planner is surprised to see the activity's Duration itself dropped from 6d to 4d, which was not intended and now conflicts with the sequencing assumptions built around the original 6-day duration.
question: Given the activity's Duration Type, is a Duration change actually the expected outcome of that Units/Time edit, or does this indicate something else is wrong – and what should the planner check first?
explanation: This is actually the expected, correct behavior for the stated Duration Type – but it reveals a misunderstanding on the resource coordinator's part, not a P6 defect. Fixed Duration & Units/Time is supposed to hold Duration and Units/Time both fixed, with total Units floating; however, that only describes what happens when total Units changes. If Units/Time itself is directly edited (as the coordinator did, changing the rate from 8h/d to 12h/d), the relationship between the three variables must still balance, and depending on which field P6 treats as the one being explicitly edited, changing Units/Time on a Fixed Duration & Units/Time activity can cause total Units to change while Duration stays fixed – so a genuine Duration change actually points to the Duration Type not truly being Fixed Duration & Units/Time as assumed, or to the edit having been made in a way that recalculated Duration instead (e.g., if the activity's Duration Type had been changed, intentionally or accidentally, to Fixed Units before the coordinator's edit). The planner's first check should be to re-confirm what Duration Type the activity is currently set to, rather than assuming the original setup is still intact.
reasoning: A Duration change from a pure Units/Time edit is the signature behavior of Fixed Units (where total Units stays fixed and Duration recalculates as rate changes), not of Fixed Duration & Units/Time (where Duration is supposed to stay fixed) – so the observed symptom is the strongest available clue that the Duration Type on this activity is not what the planner believes it to be, and must be re-verified rather than assumed from the original setup documentation.
commonMistakes: Assuming P6 made a calculation error rather than checking the actual current Duration Type setting.
Assuming Duration Type, once set, can never be changed by another user without the planner's awareness.
redFlags: Manually forces the Duration back to 6d without investigating why the Duration Type behavior didn't match expectations, leaving the underlying misconfiguration in place for the next edit.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – re-verify the current Duration Type value (it may differ from what was originally set up).
Activity Details > Resources tab – review the resource assignment's current Units/Time, Units, and Duration values to see which one actually changed.
Check the schedule log or audit trail (if enabled) for who changed the Duration Type or resource assignment and when.

skill: Distinguishing Global, Project, and Resource calendars by where they are defined and who can use them
question: In P6, what distinguishes a Global calendar from a Project calendar?

options.label: A
options.text: Global calendars are available to every project in the database; Project calendars are created within, and only usable by, one specific project

options.label: B
options.text: Global calendars can only be assigned to resources, never to activities

options.label: C
options.text: Project calendars automatically override Global calendars for every activity in that project

options.label: D
options.text: There is no real difference; both terms describe the same calendar type

explanation: Global calendars are enterprise-wide and selectable from any project in the database, making them ideal for standard company-wide working patterns (e.g., a national public holiday calendar). Project calendars are created inside a specific project and are only available for assignment within that project – another project cannot select it. Neither type of calendar automatically overrides the other; an activity or resource is simply assigned to whichever specific calendar (Global, Project, or Resource) applies to it.
reasoning: P6 calendar scope mirrors the same Global/Project distinction seen elsewhere in the platform (like Activity Codes) – broader, shared definitions at the Global level versus narrower, project-specific definitions.
commonMistakes: Assuming Project calendars automatically take precedence over Global calendars for all activities.
Believing Global calendars can't be assigned directly to activities.

skill: Identifying which calendar actually governs an activity's dates depending on its Activity Type
scenario: A planner is reviewing a tunnel boring project. Activity 'Advance TBM – Ring 450-500' is Task Dependent, assigned to the 'TBM Continuous Operations' calendar (a 7-day calendar). Activity 'Segment Lining QA Inspection' is Resource Dependent, with its Activity Calendar field also showing 'TBM Continuous Operations', but the assigned QA Inspector resource has an individual resource calendar of a 5-day week.
question: Which calendar actually governs the scheduled dates for each of these two activities?
expectedAnswer: For 'Advance TBM' (Task Dependent), the activity's own assigned Activity Calendar – 'TBM Continuous Operations' (7-day) – directly governs its scheduled dates. For 'Segment Lining QA Inspection' (Resource Dependent), the displayed Activity Calendar field is not what drives the dates; instead, the assigned QA Inspector's individual 5-day resource calendar governs the activity's scheduled dates, since Resource Dependent activities are driven by their assigned resources' own calendars.
strongAnswer: Notes that this is a common point of confusion because the Activity Calendar field is still visibly populated and shown on a Resource Dependent activity, which can mislead someone reviewing the schedule into assuming it's actually driving the dates.
expertAnswer: Adds that a QA Inspection activity being Resource Dependent and tied to a 5-day inspector calendar, while sitting inside a 7-day continuous TBM operation, could itself be a scheduling risk worth flagging – if inspection can only happen 5 days a week but the physical TBM advance is continuous, the inspection activity's dates may not actually reflect when the physical work it's inspecting occurs, which is worth raising with the project team.
explanation: Activity Type determines which calendar actually drives an activity's schedule calculation: Task Dependent uses the Activity Calendar field directly; Resource Dependent instead uses each assigned resource's own individual calendar, making the visible Activity Calendar field effectively informational only for that activity type.
reasoning: This distinction is one of the most commonly misunderstood mechanics in P6 calendar behavior, precisely because the Activity Calendar field remains visible and populated on Resource Dependent activities even though it isn't what's actually calculating the dates.
commonMistakes: Assuming the Activity Calendar field always drives dates regardless of Activity Type.
Not checking the assigned resource's individual calendar when reviewing a Resource Dependent activity's dates.
redFlags: Attempts to fix a Resource Dependent activity's dates by changing the Activity Calendar field alone, without addressing the resource's own calendar.

For the Resource Dependent activity, check Activity Details > Resources tab and the assigned resource's calendar via Enterprise > Resources > General tab.

skill: Recognizing the organization-wide risk of editing a widely-used Global calendar
scenario: A planner on a bridge rehabilitation project needs to add three project-specific working Saturdays (as calendar exceptions) to accelerate a segment of work. Rather than creating a project-specific calendar, they open the Global calendar 'Standard 5 Day Workweek' – which they know is also actively used by roughly 60 other live projects across the company – and add the three working-Saturday exceptions directly to it, planning to remove them again once this project's acceleration period is over.
question: What is the risk in this approach, and what should the planner have done instead?
expectedAnswer: Because Global calendars are shared database-wide, editing 'Standard 5 Day Workweek' directly changes the calendar for every one of the roughly 60 other live projects using it, not just this one project – those three Saturdays would become working days on every project referencing that calendar the next time each is scheduled, potentially shifting dates, float, and resource availability across unrelated projects without their planners' knowledge or consent. The planner should instead have either created a Project-specific calendar (a copy of the Global calendar with the three Saturday exceptions added only there) or, if a shared calendar was still desired, coordinated the change through whatever change-control process governs shared enterprise calendars, rather than editing the live Global calendar unilaterally.
strongAnswer: Notes that the 'remove them again afterward' plan compounds the risk – the planner also has to remember to revert the change, and any project scheduled during that in-between window is left showing the altered calendar in its history/baselines even after the exceptions are later removed.
expertAnswer: Adds that this is exactly the kind of incident that damages trust in the planning function organization-wide – even if caught quickly, other planners scheduling their projects during that window won't know their dates were affected by someone else's change, and after the fact there's no way to cleanly separate 'real' schedule movement from this side-effect without careful investigation; recommends establishing an organizational policy (e.g., Global calendars administered only by a designated scheduling administrator, with project-specific needs always handled via Project calendars).
explanation: Global calendars are, by design, shared across every project in the database that references them; editing one is never a locally-scoped action, regardless of how narrow or temporary the intended change feels. The safe, standard practice for a one-off or project-specific calendar need is to create or copy a Project-level calendar instead, leaving the shared Global calendar untouched.
reasoning: The core governance principle is that shared enterprise resources (Global calendars, and similarly Global Activity Codes) should not be edited for narrow, single-project needs, because the blast radius of the change is every project referencing that resource, not just the one the editor had in mind.
commonMistakes: Treating a Global calendar edit as equivalent in scope to a Project calendar edit.
Planning to 'temporarily' edit a shared resource and revert it later, without accounting for the interim impact on other projects scheduled during that window.
redFlags: Edits a widely-used Global calendar for a single project's narrow, temporary need without any change-control awareness or communication to other calendar users.
p6Checks: Enterprise > Calendars – check the 'Assigned to Activities/Resources' or usage indicator (where available) before editing any Global calendar to gauge how widely it's used.
Create a Project calendar (copy of the Global one) instead, and add the three working-Saturday exceptions only there.

skill: Calculating a finish date under different calendar working-day patterns for the same Original Duration
scenario: Activity 'Erect Precast Facade Panels – Zone B' has Original Duration = 12d, no constraints, and an Early Start of Monday. Ignore holidays for this calculation.
question: If the activity is assigned a Standard 5-Day calendar (Monday-Friday working, weekends non-working), on what day of the week will it finish, counting the Monday start as working day 1 of 12?
explanation: Starting Monday as working day 1, a 5-day calendar provides 5 working days per 7 calendar days. Days 1-5 = Mon-Fri (week 1). Days 6-10 = the following Mon-Fri (week 2). Days 11-12 = the Monday and Tuesday of the third week. Counting inclusively: Mon(1) Tue(2) Wed(3) Thu(4) Fri(5) | Mon(6) Tue(7) Wed(8) Thu(9) Fri(10) | Mon(11) Tue(12) - Finish falls on Tuesday of the third week.
reasoning: A 5-day calendar consumes 12 working days across 2 full working weeks (10 days) plus 2 more working days into the third week, landing on the Tuesday of that third week when the count starts on a Monday.
commonMistakes: Counting calendar days instead of working days, which would land on a different weekday entirely.
Off-by-one errors from not clearly deciding whether the start day itself counts as day 1.
p6Checks: Enterprise > Calendars – open the assigned calendar and verify its Standard Workweek pattern (which days are marked working).
After F9, check the activity's calculated Finish date directly rather than counting manually for real schedules.

skill: Predicting a successor's start date when predecessor and successor use different calendars across a weekend
scenario: On an industrial park roadworks project, activity 'Pour Concrete Pavement – Section 9' is on a 6-Day calendar (Monday-Saturday working) and has a Finish-to-Start relationship (0 lag) to successor activity 'Saw-Cut Control Joints', which is assigned a 5-Day calendar (Monday-Friday working). The predecessor's calculated Finish lands on a Saturday.
question: On which day will the successor 'Saw-Cut Control Joints' actually be scheduled to start, and why might a planner initially expect it to start on that same Saturday?
explanation: The successor will start on the following Monday, not the Saturday the predecessor finishes on, because P6 schedules a Finish-to-Start relationship's successor to begin at the next available working period according to the SUCCESSOR's own calendar – and Saturday is a non-working day on the successor's 5-Day calendar, even though it was a working day for the predecessor. A planner might initially (incorrectly) expect the successor to start immediately on Saturday because that's when the predecessor physically finishes, forgetting that the successor's own calendar – not the predecessor's – governs when the successor's earliest start can actually occur.

skill: Explaining why Total Float values can look inconsistent across paths that use different calendars
scenario: On a petrochemical plant turnaround, two parallel paths both feed the same downstream milestone. Path A consists entirely of activities on the 'Standard 5-Day' calendar; Path B consists entirely of activities on a '24-Hour Continuous' calendar (used for a shutdown-critical unit that runs around the clock). After scheduling, an experienced scheduler notices that comparing the Total Float values shown on Path A activities against Path B activities doesn't behave as intuitively expected when trying to judge which path is 'more critical' at a glance, even though both ultimately tie into the same milestone.
question: Why can Total Float values be difficult to compare directly across activities on very different calendars like these, and what should the scheduler do instead of comparing the raw numbers at face value?
explanation: Each activity's Total Float is calculated and expressed in the working-time units of that specific activity's own assigned calendar, not in a single universal calendar-day scale – so a Total Float value on a 5-Day-calendar activity and a Total Float value on a 24-Hour-calendar activity are not directly comparable the way two numbers on the same calendar would be, because a 'day' of float means a different amount of real elapsed time (and a different amount of actual available working time) on each. A scheduler should not simply eyeball and rank raw float values across mixed-calendar paths as if they were on the same scale; instead, they should rely on the calculated critical/near-critical flags (or the Longest Path method) that P6 already derives correctly from the underlying date math, and where a manual sanity check across paths is genuinely needed, compare using actual calendar dates (the real Late Finish minus Early Finish elapsed time) rather than the displayed float-day counts alone.
reasoning: Float is fundamentally a duration value (Late minus Early dates) converted into the display units of the activity's own calendar; mixing calendars with very different working-time density (a 5-day week versus a continuous 24-hour operation) means the same underlying real time gap can produce very different-looking float-day counts on each path, which is a well-known source of confusion on schedules that deliberately mix calendars for genuinely different operational reasons.
commonMistakes: Assuming Total Float is always expressed on a single universal time scale across an entire schedule.
Concluding one path is definitively 'more critical' than another purely by comparing raw float-day numbers without checking the underlying calendars.
redFlags: Reports to management that Path A is 'safer' than Path B purely based on a larger displayed float-day number, without checking whether the two paths are even on comparable calendars.
p6Checks: Activity Details > General tab – confirm the calendar assigned to representative activities on each path.
Compare actual Late Finish and Early Finish calendar dates directly rather than only the displayed float-day count.
Use the Critical filter / Longest Path setting (Schedule Options) as the authoritative measure of criticality rather than manually ranking float values.

skill: Understanding that a Resource Dependent activity's overall duration is driven by the slowest-available assigned resource

Because the activity is Resource Dependent, each resource's 6 working days are measured against that resource's own calendar independently: the Crane Operator's 6 working days consume only 6 calendar days (since every day is working on a 7-day calendar), while the Torque Technician's 6 working days will span more calendar days once a weekend falls inside that window (since Saturday/Sunday are non-working on their 5-day calendar). The overall activity is scheduled to encompass whichever resource takes the longest in real calendar time, so here the Torque Technician's assignment – despite being 'equal' in working-day terms – ends up driving the activity's actual finish date later than the Crane Operator's assignment alone would.

skill: Explaining how an LOE activity's own calendar affects its displayed duration relative to the driving activities on a different calendar

reasoning: LOE duration is a calculated output, but it's still expressed in the activity's own calendar's working-day units, not in raw calendar days or the driving activities' calendar units – so mixing calendars between an LOE activity and the work it's tracking produces a duration number that doesn't intuitively match the calendar-day span most people would expect, purely because of the difference in working-day density between the two calendars.

Not considering that Duration display units depend on the LOE activity's own assigned calendar.

explanation: Multi-subcontractor integrated schedules routinely bring together several independently-maintained calendars, each reflecting different real working patterns and holiday sets; a schedule quality review specifically needs to verify these calendars are each individually accurate, that they're consistently updated for site-wide events, and that interface points between subcontractors don't silently create unrealistic immediate-transition assumptions because of a calendar mismatch.

skill: Recognizing that P6 does not require the Data Date to fall on a working day of any particular calendar

explanation: Yes, this is possible and is not restricted by P6. The Data Date is simply the 'as of' status point for the schedule and is not required to fall on a working day of any particular calendar – P6 will accept a Data Date on a non-working day without error. What it does mean practically is that any remaining work will be scheduled to resume at the next available working period after that Sunday according to each activity's own calendar (e.g., the following Monday on a 5-Day calendar), since no actual work is expected to occur on the non-working Sunday itself.
reasoning: The Data Date is a status/reference point, not itself a scheduled work period, so it has no dependency on any calendar's working/non-working pattern; the calendars only come into play when P6 calculates where remaining work can actually occur relative to that Data Date.

Assuming setting Data Date to a non-working day somehow shifts reported progress dates incorrectly.

skill: Diagnosing a budgeted-hours discrepancy caused by a mismatch between Admin Preferences Time Periods and a calendar's actual defined workday length

A resource is assigned to a 5-day-duration activity at 100% Units, and the planner expects Budgeted Labor Units to equal 50 hours (5 days x 10 hours). Instead, P6 shows Budgeted Units as 40 hours.
question: What is the most likely cause of this discrepancy between the expected 50 hours and the displayed 40 hours, and where would the planner check to confirm it?
explanation: The most likely cause is a mismatch between the calendar's actual defined hours-per-day (10 hours, correctly set on the Project calendar itself) and the database-wide 'Hours per Day' conversion factor set in Admin Preferences > Time Periods (likely still at the common default of 8 hours per day). Certain unit/duration conversions and displayed totals in P6 rely on the Admin Preferences Time Periods conversion factors rather than re-reading the specific calendar's actual workday length every time, so if that global setting still says 8 hours per day while the calendar itself is configured for 10-hour days, budgeted-hours figures can be calculated or displayed using the mismatched 8-hour assumption (5 days x 8 hours = 40), producing exactly this kind of discrepancy.
reasoning: P6 maintains two conceptually separate places where 'hours per day' can be defined: the specific calendar's own Standard Workweek hours (used for actual date/duration scheduling), and the database-wide Admin Preferences Time Periods conversion factors (used for certain unit-of-measure conversions and displays); when a project's real shift length deviates from the generic 8-hour default but Admin Preferences was never updated to match, budgeted-hours math that leans on the Time Periods factor will disagree with what the calendar itself implies.
commonMistakes: Assuming Budgeted Units are always calculated purely from the assigned calendar's actual hours-per-day setting.
Not checking Admin Preferences at all, since it's a less frequently visited settings area than the calendar dialog itself.
redFlags: Manually adjusts the resource's Units/Time or Units values to force the number to 50 without identifying and correcting the actual Admin Preferences mismatch, leaving the root cause to keep producing wrong figures on other activities.

skill: Deciding when a 24-hour (continuous) calendar is the appropriate choice versus a standard working calendar

expectedAnswer: 'Kiln Refractory Curing' is the appropriate candidate for a 24-Hour calendar: the curing process itself continues physically around the clock regardless of whether crews are present, so representing it on a calendar with every hour of every day as working time correctly reflects that the clock never stops on this activity. 'Structural Steel Erection – Silo Bay' should stay on a standard working calendar (matching the site's actual shift pattern), since it genuinely only progresses when crews are present and working, and a 24-Hour calendar would incorrectly imply continuous progress happening even during hours no one is actually erecting steel.

skill: Distinguishing the Standard Workweek pattern from date-specific Exceptions when adding a one-off working Saturday
scenario: A project normally runs a Standard 5-Day calendar (Monday-Friday working, weekends non-working). To recover three days of slippage, the site works a single overtime Saturday two weeks from now, then returns to the normal 5-Day pattern the following week.
question: Should the planner change the calendar's Standard Workweek pattern to include Saturday as a working day, or use a different mechanism? Explain the correct approach.
expectedAnswer: The planner should add that one specific Saturday as a working-day Exception on the calendar, not change the Standard Workweek pattern itself. The Standard Workweek defines the recurring, ongoing weekly pattern (which would make every Saturday going forward a working day if changed, not just the intended one-off date); Exceptions override the standard pattern for individual, specific calendar dates without altering the recurring weekly template. Since only this one particular Saturday needs to be working, an Exception is the correct, narrowly-scoped tool.
strongAnswer: Notes that changing the Standard Workweek by mistake would silently make every future Saturday a working day, which would distort every activity's date calculations across the rest of the project, not just the intended recovery week.
expertAnswer: Adds that this same Exception-based approach is also how holidays are added (as non-working Exceptions) – the Standard Workweek and Exceptions are two complementary tools: recurring weekly pattern versus specific-date overrides in either direction (making a normally non-working day working, or a normally working day non-working).
explanation: P6 calendars are built from two layers: a Standard Workweek (the recurring weekly working/non-working pattern) and Exceptions (specific calendar dates that override that pattern, in either direction). A genuinely recurring change belongs in the Standard Workweek; a one-off date-specific change belongs as an Exception.
reasoning: Using the wrong layer for a one-off change (editing the Standard Workweek for something that should be a single-date Exception) has an unintended blast radius – it doesn't just affect the one date the planner cared about, it silently changes every future occurrence of that weekday for the rest of the calendar's life.
commonMistakes: Editing the Standard Workweek to make Saturday working, unintentionally making every future Saturday a working day.
Assuming Exceptions and the Standard Workweek pattern are the same setting.
redFlags: Changes the Standard Workweek for what is clearly described as a single one-off recovery day.
p6Checks: Enterprise > Calendars – open the calendar, navigate to the specific Saturday date in the calendar grid, and mark it as a working Exception (rather than touching the Standard Workweek tab).
Confirm the following Saturday (the week after) remains correctly non-working, proving the Exception didn't affect the recurring pattern.
